To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
saccades made to remembered target locations are sufficient to activate retinal coordinates in human visual cortex, even when no saccades are actually made.
the visual cortex of the human brain is activated when a saccadic eye movement is executed, even if the target location is remembered and not visible.

saccades executed to a remembered target location can produce a spatially specific activation in the contralaterally located human visual cortex, and that this is also the case even if the saccades are not actually executed.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between visual attention and the brain, and in particular the role played by the early visual areas.
the neural mechanisms that underlie the control of saccadic eye movements.
the neural correlates of visual spatial attention and visual working memory.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the saccadic eye movements are not necessary and sufficient conditions to activate retinopically visual cortex, and that other mechanisms are also involved.
the saccade to remembered location is sufficient to activate the retinotopic cortex spatially corresponding with the remembered target location.
the activation of the early visual cortex in the present study is not the result of the saccade per se but is due to the fact that the visual target was remembered.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the saccadic eye movements to a remembered location activate the corresponding retinotopic regions in visual cortex, and that this spatially specific activation can occur without a saccade.
the visual cortex is not a passive recipient of sensory input, but rather is actively engaged by the brain to maintain the integrity of the sensory world.
saccades can activate visual cortex, even in the absence of a visual stimulus.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the spatially specific activations in retinotopic cortex that we observed are consistent with a model of saccadic memory that involves the activation of a “saccadic map” that is spatially specific to the target location and is maintained by the saccade itself.
the visual cortex is more plastic than previously thought, and that the plasticity can be driven not by visual stimuli, but by eye movements.
saccades are not just about the eyes moving, and that the visual system can use saccades to maintain spatially specific representations in early visual cortex.
